title: A Long Route in Short Legs

scenes.tts: In a grasshopper embryo, a young leg is growing. The first axons set out for the central nervous system. No other axons are ahead of them. There is nothing to follow. Yet kill one guidepost cell before they get there, and they lose their way. So how does a growth cone know which way to go?
scenes.visual: A faint leg-shaped corridor; two growth cones at the far end; the central nervous system at the other end; question marks along the empty route.
scenes.narration: In a grasshopper embryo, a young leg is growing. The first axons set out for the central nervous system. No other axons are ahead of them. There is nothing to follow. Yet kill one guidepost cell before they get there, and they lose their way. So how does a growth cone know which way to go?

scenes.tts: The growth cone does not carry a map. It reads its surroundings one stretch at a time. A long route is hard to steer in one go, so it is cut into short legs. A trail with signposts is easy to follow. Axons use the same trick. The first axons through a territory are called pioneers. Along their route sit guidepost cells. At a guidepost, the growth cone stops, reads, and changes course.
scenes.visual: A crossed-out map; the route splits into four short legs; yellow guideposts appear at the turns; pioneer growth cones pause at each one and turn.
scenes.narration: The growth cone does not carry a map. It reads its surroundings one stretch at a time. A long route is hard to steer in one go, so it is cut into short legs. A trail with signposts is easy to follow. Axons use the same trick. The first axons through a territory are called pioneers. Along their route sit guidepost cells. At a guidepost, the growth cone stops, reads, and changes course.

scenes.tts: The first axons belong to a pair of nerve cells called T i one. The route has several turns, and at one sits a group of guidepost cells called C x one. The growth cones touch them just before they turn. Bentley and Caudy asked whether the growth cones need them. They destroyed C x one with focused light before the growth cones arrived.

scenes.tts: Then the pioneers failed to take the normal route. They sent branches in abnormal directions. The conclusion is narrow, and that is its strength. At this turn, in this preparation, that cell is needed. The experiment does not say whether the cell provides adhesion or a signal.
scenes.visual: Pioneers reach the empty turn and send red branches in wrong directions; the text says the cell is needed here; two question chips, adhesion and signal.
scenes.narration: Then the pioneers failed to take the normal route. They sent branches in abnormal directions. The conclusion is narrow, and that is its strength. At this turn, in this preparation, that cell is needed. The experiment does not say whether the cell provides adhesion or a signal.

scenes.tts: Later work found that the full route is built from several legs. They are read partly from guideposts, and partly from boundaries in the surrounding tissue. A guidepost is one important cue among several. Later axons, called followers, often grow along the pioneers.
scenes.visual: The legs light up; guideposts pulse; grey tissue boundaries appear across the corridor; purple follower axons grow along the pioneers.
scenes.narration: Later work found that the full route is built from several legs. They are read partly from guideposts, and partly from boundaries in the surrounding tissue. A guidepost is one important cue among several. Later axons, called followers, often grow along the pioneers.

scenes.tts: So a growth cone does not steer a whole route at once. It reads its surroundings one stretch at a time, and some of what it reads is other cells. In the grasshopper leg, remove one guidepost, and the pioneers lose their normal route at that turn. Keep this rule: a long route is steered in short legs.
scenes.visual: Legs light one after another; guideposts pulse; one guidepost is crossed out and the axon beyond it is lost; the intact route returns under the rule.
